clips.end_words: Don't buy anything from that company ever again
clips.caption:
Kevin Trudeau says most pills need a coating once they're pressed, so they don't crumble in the bottle - and one of the most common coatings in the industry is shellac, the same resin used to finish wood.

His story: a family of four on a septic system found thousands of undigested vitamin pills in the tank when they switched to city plumbing. The pills had passed straight through, coating and all, without ever breaking down.

His rule: skip pressed pills. For capsules, check the ingredient list for 'cellulose capsule' or 'organic cellulose capsule' - anything else is likely a plastic-based shell.

clips.end_words: the food has to be whole food concentrates
clips.caption:
Kevin Trudeau says there's a reason eating an orange works better than drinking the juice: the fiber in the whole fruit slows everything down.

His point: that slower pace lets more of the vitamin C and bioflavonoids get absorbed in the intestine instead of the stomach. Skip the fiber and drink straight juice, he says, and more of it breaks down too fast - which can even leave you with extra stomach acid.

His line for it: animals in the wild don't have juice machines.

Fruit or juice - which do you reach for first?

clips.end_words: no nutritional value in our soil anymore
clips.caption:
Kevin Trudeau says the onions he grew up with made the whole house cry when you cut them open - today's onions, he says, you can chop all day and barely smell.

His explanation: the soil most produce is grown in now carries far less nutritional value than it used to. Part of the reason traces back to the 1930s Dust Bowl, when drought turned the topsoil in America's farm belt to dust and blew away roughly 12 feet of it - the exact layer that held the minerals.

His takeaway: flavor is a rough proxy for nutrition. A food with almost no smell or taste may be giving you almost nothing else either.
